_meta.fields: term, def (one plain sentence), why (one line), related (ids), aka (other names), kind: 'fact' = accounting or legal definition; 'heuristic' = market shorthand or rule of thumb, not an official measure.

treasury.def: The government department that collects taxes, makes payments and borrows by selling securities to cover the gap.
treasury.why: Every dollar of federal debt starts as a Treasury auction.

deficit.def: Spending minus revenue in a given year; the deficit is what adds to the debt.
deficit.why: About $2.0T in FY2026, so Treasury must sell about that much new debt on net.

gross-debt.def: All Treasury debt: what the public holds plus what government trust funds hold.
gross-debt.why: The headline '$40 trillion' number; it is also roughly what the debt limit counts.

debt-held-by-public.def: Treasury debt owned by anyone outside the federal government, including the Federal Reserve, foreigners, funds and households.
debt-held-by-public.why: Economists prefer this measure because it is debt the government owes to someone else.

intragovernmental-debt.def: Special non-tradable Treasury securities held by federal trust funds such as Social Security and Medicare.
intragovernmental-debt.why: This is the government owing itself, about $7.7T; it signals future benefit obligations, not market borrowing.

marketable-debt.def: Treasury securities that can be bought and sold in the market: bills, notes, bonds, TIPS and FRNs.
marketable-debt.why: This is the about $31.8T stock that markets price, trade and finance in repo.

non-marketable-debt.def: Treasury debt that can't be resold: trust-fund securities, savings bonds (Series EE/I) sold to individuals, and securities issued to state and local governments.
non-marketable-debt.why: Counts toward gross debt and the debt limit, but never trades.

t-bill.def: Short-term Treasury debt (4 to 52 weeks) sold at a discount and repaid at face value, with no coupon.
t-bill.why: Bills reprice to current rates within weeks, so their share decides how fast rate changes hit interest costs.

cash-management-bill.def: An off-schedule bill Treasury sells to cover short cash gaps, often around tax dates or after a debt-limit fix.
cash-management-bill.why: CMB bursts are how Treasury rebuilds the TGA quickly, which pulls cash out of markets.

note.def: Treasury debt with a fixed coupon paid twice a year, maturing in 2, 3, 5, 7 or 10 years.
note.why: Notes are about half of marketable debt and lock in a rate for years.

bond.def: Long-term Treasury debt with a fixed coupon, maturing in 20 or 30 years.
bond.why: The 'long end': it is the most sensitive to inflation and fiscal worries.
aka: the long end (10–30y part of the curve)

tips.def: Treasury debt whose principal rises with CPI inflation; the coupon is a fixed 'real' rate on that growing principal.
tips.why: TIPS yields are the market's main reading of real interest rates.

frn.def: Two-year Treasury debt whose interest resets weekly to the latest 13-week bill auction rate, plus a fixed spread.
frn.why: Economically it behaves like a bill, which adds to Treasury's short-rate exposure.

aka: X-date (the day cash and extraordinary measures run out)
debt-ceiling.def: A dollar cap set by Congress on how much debt Treasury may have outstanding; currently $41.104T, set July 2025.
debt-ceiling.why: Standoffs drain then refill the TGA, a predictable swing in market liquidity.

extraordinary-measures.def: Accounting moves, such as pausing investments in some federal pension funds, that free room under the debt limit for a while.
extraordinary-measures.why: They let Treasury keep paying bills for months after hitting the limit.

auction.def: The sale of new Treasury securities to bidders, on a fixed public calendar; everyone pays the same highest accepted yield.
auction.why: Weak auctions are watched as a real-time read of demand for US debt.

quarterly-refunding.def: Treasury's announcement every three months (Feb, May, Aug, Nov) of borrowing needs and the coupon sizes it plans to sell.
quarterly-refunding.why: Shifting issuance between bills and longer debt moves term premium and market liquidity.

tbac.def: A committee of dealers and investors that advises Treasury at each refunding.
tbac.why: TBAC suggests bills stay around 15–20% of marketable debt; they are about 22% now.

primary-dealer.def: One of about 25 banks and broker-dealers that must bid at every Treasury auction and trade directly with the New York Fed.
primary-dealer.why: Dealers absorb whatever others don't buy, so their balance-sheet room matters in stress.

bid-to-cover.def: Total bids at an auction divided by the amount sold.
bid-to-cover.why: A falling ratio hints at weaker demand, though one reading means little.

tail.def: When an auction clears at a higher yield than the market expected just before it.
tail.why: A big tail means buyers had to be paid extra, often read as a warning sign.

buyback.def: Treasury buying back older, less-traded securities before maturity, usually paid for by issuing new ones.
buyback.why: Supports market liquidity and helps Treasury smooth its cash; it doesn't shrink the debt much.

tga.def: Treasury's checking account at the Federal Reserve; tax receipts and auction proceeds go in, government payments go out.
tga.why: When the TGA rises, bank reserves fall by the same amount, all else equal.

tga-rebuild.def: A stretch, usually after a debt-limit deal, when Treasury issues extra bills to refill its cash account.
tga-rebuild.why: Pulls hundreds of billions of reserves or RRP cash out of markets in weeks.

federal-reserve.def: The US central bank, which sets short-term interest rates and creates bank reserves.
federal-reserve.why: Its balance sheet is the base layer of all dollar plumbing.

fed-balance-sheet.def: The Fed's assets (mostly Treasuries and mortgage bonds) and liabilities (currency, reserves, TGA, reverse repos); the two sides are always equal.
fed-balance-sheet.why: If one liability grows, another must shrink unless assets grow, which is the key identity of the plumbing.

soma.def: The Fed's portfolio of Treasuries and agency mortgage-backed securities, run by the New York Fed.
soma.why: About $6.3T; it makes the Fed the single largest holder of Treasuries.

reserves.def: Deposits that banks keep at the Fed; they are the money banks use to pay each other.
reserves.why: Reserves are the scarce input for repo and bank lending; too few and funding rates spike.

currency-in-circulation.def: Paper dollars and coins held outside the Fed and Treasury, recorded as a liability of the Fed.
currency-in-circulation.why: Grows steadily, about $2.4T, and slowly absorbs reserves.

on-rrp.def: A Fed facility where money funds and others can deposit cash overnight against Treasury collateral at a set rate.
on-rrp.why: It was a $2.5T cash 'reservoir' in 2022; now near zero, so new drains hit reserves directly.

foreign-repo-pool.def: Reverse repos the Fed offers foreign central banks so they can park dollars overnight.
foreign-repo-pool.why: About $325B; it is most of the 'reverse repo' line on the Fed's balance sheet now.

fed-funds-rate.def: The overnight rate banks charge each other for unsecured loans of reserves; the Fed sets a target range for it (3.75–4.00% now).
fed-funds-rate.why: The anchor for almost every short-term dollar rate.

iorb.def: The rate the Fed pays banks on reserves (3.90% now).
iorb.why: The Fed's main tool for steering short rates: banks won't lend reserves for less.

rate-corridor.def: The band of Fed rates that boxes in overnight rates: the ON RRP rate sets the floor, standing repo the ceiling, and IORB sits in between.
rate-corridor.why: Where SOFR sits inside the band shows how plentiful cash is.

srf.def: A Fed facility that lends cash overnight to dealers and banks against Treasuries or mortgage bonds at the top of the corridor.
srf.why: Caps repo rate spikes; heavy use (a $74.6B record at end-2025) signals cash is tight.

discount-window.def: The Fed's lending facility for banks, secured by a wide range of collateral.
discount-window.why: A backstop that banks are reluctant to use because borrowing can look like a sign of trouble.

fima-repo.def: Lets foreign central banks borrow dollars overnight from the Fed using their Treasuries as collateral, instead of selling them.
fima-repo.why: Prevents forced foreign selling of Treasuries during a dollar crunch.

swap-lines.def: Agreements under which the Fed swaps dollars for another central bank's currency so it can lend dollars to its own banks.
swap-lines.why: The global lender-of-last-resort channel for offshore dollar stress (2008, 2020).

qe.def: The Fed buying large amounts of Treasuries and mortgage bonds with newly created reserves.
qe.why: It grows reserves and removes duration from the market, pushing long yields down.

qt.def: The Fed shrinking its portfolio by letting securities mature without replacing them.
qt.why: It drained the ON RRP first, then reserves; it ended Dec 1, 2025.

reserve-management-purchases.def: Fed purchases of T-bills meant only to keep reserves ample as currency and the TGA grow, not to ease policy.
reserve-management-purchases.why: Mechanically they add reserves like QE, but they buy bills rather than duration, which is why the Fed says they are not QE.

ample-reserves.def: The Fed's target state where reserves are plentiful enough that small changes don't move short rates much.
ample-reserves.why: 'No longer ample' means repo rates start trading above IORB, as they have at times in late 2026.

deferred-asset.def: An IOU the Fed books when its interest costs exceed its income; it must earn this back before sending profits to Treasury again.
deferred-asset.why: About $236B. Until it's paid down, the Fed sends Treasury almost none of the $55–110B a year in profits it remitted in 2019–21.

aka: reverse repo (the cash lender's side of the same trade)
repo.def: A short-term loan in which one side sells a Treasury and agrees to buy it back tomorrow at a slightly higher price, like a pawn shop for bonds.
repo.why: Trillions a day of repo let investors hold Treasuries with borrowed cash.

sofr.def: The average rate on overnight repo backed by Treasuries, published daily by the New York Fed from about $3T of trades.
sofr.why: It replaced LIBOR as the benchmark for loans and derivatives; SOFR above IORB signals tight cash.

tri-party-repo.def: Repo where a clearing bank (BNY) holds the collateral and handles settlement between the two sides.
tri-party-repo.why: Where money funds lend; it is also how the ON RRP and standing repo settle.

cleared-repo.def: Repo that goes through the Fixed Income Clearing Corporation (FICC), a central counterparty, which lets offsetting trades be netted.
cleared-repo.why: Netting saves dealer balance sheet; the SEC mandate pushes most Treasury repo here by mid-2027.

bilateral-repo.def: Repo negotiated directly between two firms with no clearing house, often with little or no haircut.
bilateral-repo.why: Where much hedge-fund leverage sits, and the least visible part of the market.

haircut.def: The discount a lender applies to collateral; a 2% haircut means lending $98 against $100 of bonds.
haircut.why: Low haircuts allow high leverage, and rising haircuts force deleveraging.

money-market-fund.def: A fund holding very short, safe assets (bills, repo, ON RRP) that savers treat like cash; about $7.9T.
money-market-fund.why: MMFs choose between bills, private repo and the ON RRP based on which pays most, and that choice moves liquidity.

bank-deposits.def: Money households and firms hold at commercial banks; it is a liability of the bank, backed in part by reserves.
bank-deposits.why: When a deposit holder buys a bill, deposits and reserves both shrink as cash moves to the TGA.

unrealized-losses.def: Drops in the market value of bonds a bank still holds; they don't count against capital unless the bonds are sold, or are marked as available for sale.
unrealized-losses.why: Rate hikes created large losses on bank bond holdings, which turned into a run at SVB in 2023.

btfp.def: An emergency Fed program (2023–24) that lent to banks against Treasuries valued at face value rather than market value.
btfp.why: It stopped the 2023 bank runs by making underwater bonds full collateral.

slr.def: A capital rule requiring big banks to hold capital against all assets, even safe Treasuries and reserves.
slr.why: It limited how many Treasuries dealers could hold; the April 2026 reform loosened it.

basis-trade.def: Hedge funds buy cash Treasuries, sell matching futures, and fund the bonds in repo, earning the small price gap many times over with leverage.
basis-trade.why: About $2T in size; when it unwinds quickly (2020, April 2025) Treasuries get dumped all at once.

swap-spread.def: The difference between an interest-rate swap rate and the Treasury yield of the same maturity.
swap-spread.why: Negative swap spreads show Treasuries are cheap because dealers lack room to hold them; leveraged trades bet on this.

central-clearing-mandate.def: An SEC rule requiring most Treasury cash trades (by Dec 31, 2026) and repo (by Jun 30, 2027) to go through a central clearing house.
central-clearing-mandate.why: Aims to make the market safer and more nettable, and changes how hedge funds and dealers finance positions.

tic-data.def: Treasury's monthly survey of cross-border holdings and flows of securities.
tic-data.why: The source for 'Japan holds $1.07T'; it records where securities are held, not who ultimately owns them.

foreign-official.def: Foreign central banks and governments that hold Treasuries, mostly as currency reserves.
foreign-official.why: Now about 41% of foreign holdings, down from most; private foreign buyers are more price-sensitive.

eurodollar.def: Dollar deposits and loans held at banks outside the US, outside direct Fed control.
eurodollar.why: Trillions of offshore dollar debt means global stress becomes a scramble for dollars.

cross-currency-basis.def: The extra cost of borrowing dollars by swapping another currency, compared with borrowing them directly.
cross-currency-basis.why: A widening basis is the price signal of a global dollar shortage.

carry-trade.def: Borrowing in low-rate yen to invest in higher-yielding assets, including US Treasuries.
carry-trade.why: When Japanese rates rise or the yen jumps, carry unwinds can force selling of US assets.

boj.def: Japan's central bank; its policy rate is 1.25% after the Sep 2026 hike, the highest since 1995.
boj.why: Higher JGB yields give Japanese investors, the largest foreign holders of Treasuries, a reason to stay home.

stablecoin.def: A crypto token meant to stay worth $1, backed by a reserve of cash and short Treasuries held by the issuer.
stablecoin.why: About $300B in supply; issuers like Tether and Circle are now among the larger T-bill holders.

genius-act.def: The July 2025 US law regulating payment stablecoins; reserves must be 1:1 in cash, deposits, Treasuries maturing within 93 days, short repo, or government MMFs.
genius-act.why: It makes stablecoin growth a structural source of demand for T-bills.

net-liquidity.def: A trader rule of thumb: Fed total assets minus the TGA minus the ON RRP.
net-liquidity.why: Popular for explaining stock and bitcoin moves; it is not an official measure and its correlation with prices is debated.

liquidity.def: Loose shorthand for how much cash and easy funding is sloshing around for investors to buy assets with.
liquidity.why: Used in many incompatible ways: reserves, money supply, credit conditions, market depth. Always ask which one.

real-yield.def: The interest rate after inflation, read directly from TIPS yields.
real-yield.why: High real yields raise the cost of holding non-yielding assets like gold or bitcoin, at least in theory.

dxy.def: The dollar's value against a basket of six major currencies, mostly the euro.
dxy.why: A strong dollar tightens conditions for anyone abroad with dollar debts.

term-premium.def: The extra yield investors demand to lock money in a long bond instead of rolling bills; it can only be estimated with models.
term-premium.why: 'Term premium is rising' is how markets express worry about supply, inflation or fiscal risk.

yield-curve.def: Yields on Treasuries plotted from shortest to longest maturity.
yield-curve.why: Its slope shows market expectations for growth, inflation and Fed policy.

duration.def: How much a bond's price moves when yields change; a duration of 8 means about an 8% price drop for each 1-point rise in yields.
duration.why: Who holds the duration is who takes the losses when rates rise.

bond-vigilantes.def: A nickname for investors who sell government bonds and push yields up to protest loose fiscal or monetary policy.
bond-vigilantes.why: A narrative, not an organized group, but rising term premium is how it would show up.

fiscal-dominance.def: A situation where government debt is so large that the central bank feels pressure to keep rates low to keep interest costs manageable.
fiscal-dominance.why: Economists disagree on whether the US is near it; it is a core 'debasement' argument in the bitcoin world.

rollover-risk.def: The risk that maturing debt must be refinanced at higher rates, or in a market that doesn't want it.
rollover-risk.why: About a third of marketable debt matures within a year. The weighted average maturity is about 71 months.

turning-over-bills.def: Paying off maturing bills by selling new ones, done every week, worth trillions a year.
turning-over-bills.why: Routine, but it means bill rates feed through to Treasury's interest bill within months.

net-interest.def: Interest the government pays on debt held by the public, minus interest it earns; about $1.05T in FY2026.
net-interest.why: About 14% of federal spending, and CBO projects it rising toward 19% by 2036.

quarter-end.def: Banks, especially foreign ones, shrink their balance sheets on reporting dates, pulling back from repo.
quarter-end.why: Causes predictable repo rate spikes and standing repo usage on the last day of each quarter.

rrp-drained.def: Shorthand for the ON RRP falling from $2.5T (2022) to near zero by 2025.
rrp-drained.why: With the cushion gone, any new TGA build or QT drains bank reserves directly.

t-bill-and-chill.def: Slang for parking cash in T-bills or money funds to earn about 4% with no risk.
t-bill-and-chill.why: Explains the growth of money funds to $7.9T and the strong demand for bills.
